chapter: Mary Collins on Jelly Roll Morton and Willie the Lion
title: Mary lived with Jelly Roll Morton and Mabel in New York
summary: Mary recalls nine months in Morton's household, his ambition and fame, and friend Charles Edward Smith.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: I put one line in there. It got a part in there about they didn't know how to wear their pegs. I told him, I said, in the joints in Storyville where Janice sat and played, I said, you couldn't even come in the joint because they didn't find out how much lying you was. Did you ever hear him play down here at all? No, no. See, before he died, about eight months before he died, I lived with him and his wife for nine months in New York. I never knew him before, but when I went to New York, I made a point in my mind that I was going to see him. So he was living on 130 feet between 7th and 8th Avenue at a woman's house near New York. She had a rooming house up there. And Janice was living with a woman they called Mabel. Mabel Morton. Now he was, and he wrote a number for her called Posse Mabel. Well, I mean, I had it all night. Him and her, I, her and him used to go to a church every Sunday. Well, I really thought that he was his wife until after his death in California when young comes some man needed somebody. Yeah, man needed, yeah. So I didn't know who, how, how this whole situation was complicated, you know. But I always knew it ought to be Mabel Morton. Yeah. And, uh, I lived in the same house with him, I mean, and I was just with him every day. I went down on the Clarence Williams off. No, he was an erratic cat, man. You know what I mean? Oh, man, he knocked me out. You know what I mean? Yeah. Well, you see what it is. And so, you see what bring about a jealous way is, I mean, they were quite queer to a lot of people. But I understand him thoroughly because for the simple reason why he, he was the George Gershwin of his day. You got to give the man the recognition that he would really, but, but he wanted it so bad and looked like that he just couldn't attain the objective. He wanted to see his name in lights more than anybody you know. He just, he just loved fame. He just loved being the top man. He wasn't going to play second fiddle for nobody. You could bet that. And he'd get up on Broadway and they'd go to talking about various forms of music. Various forms. Well, what do you mean? There isn't but one music, jealous music. Yeah, it's all jelly roll. Boy, he used to knock me out there. That's what you mean, various forms. There's only one music, jelly rolls music.
Did you get along with him all right?

Yeah, I got along with him fine. He used to have a white boy who comes to the house every day. He's a great writer. Him and I got to be good friends. His name is Charles Edward Smith. Yeah, I can say that. Boy, he was crazy about jelly. He was that, man, he was, and Mabel could cook all kind of Creole gumbo and everything. We had us a ball every day up there. I got a manuscript he gave me with a number. I was trying to figure, Mr. Russell, when you said finger breaker, I've got that manuscript, jelly, give it to me. That sounds right. Yeah, I've got it home on a piece of manuscript paper. About seven or eight bars of the piano solo. And it's got jelly roll more than his name on it. He's right when he said jelly roll there.
